A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same category-extrapolation research, and their supplied text, equations, tables, and figures are readable. Neither contains an appendix, although v3 references one for additional visualizations, implementation settings, and method comparisons. Those references leave identifiable gaps in the comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original granularity experiments, benchmark evaluations on three datasets, component ablations, sensitivity studies, and feature visualizations.

after.justification: v3 retains original benchmark and pilot-study results and reports additional random-versus-selected auxiliary-data controls in Tables 2 and 6.

M1.justification: Section 3.1 revises the explicit LLM prompt from requesting visually similar classes to requesting related fine-grained categories. This changes the documented category-search input; the filtering framework, neighbor-silencing loss, and classifier masking remain unchanged. The PDFs do not establish whether auxiliary data were regenerated.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate ImageNet-LT, iNaturalist 2018, and Places-LT and use the ImageNet-21k/OpenImages pool for the granularity pilot. The added random-versus-selected data controls introduce no identified new benchmark, domain, or task.

E2.justification: v3 Table 2 adds RD and SD controls to the corresponding baseline comparisons. Its main comparison tables also omit many v1 comparators, including the separate RAC comparison. However, v3 redirects further method comparisons to an unavailable appendix, preventing a reliable assessment of the overall comparator-set change. The DINOv2 LiVT/Bal-CE relabeling alone does not establish a new comparator.

E3.justification: v3 adds random-versus-selected auxiliary-data control conditions and revises the component comparison in Table 6. The reported backbone, training epochs, batch size, augmentations, accuracy metrics, and class-frequency groups remain unchanged. Newly specified filtering thresholds are additional disclosure, not evidence of changed experimental settings.

E4.justification: Tables 2 and 6 add a systematic test of whether auxiliary-data benefits depend on selecting neighboring categories rather than merely adding images, addressing a central question about the method. Table 6 also replaces the earlier separate neighbor-silencing, direct-classifier, and combined rows with data-selection and component rows. The original granularity study, sensitivity plots, and feature visualizations remain.

E5.justification: Both versions state that five pilot experiments are averaged in Section 2.2. The supplied benchmark results retain the same reporting practice, without added seed information, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests.

E6.justification: Numerous auxiliary-data baseline results are revised, reversing their overall trend: scratch LiVT† accuracy changes from 59.3 to 65.2 on ImageNet-LT and from 66.2 to 77.0 on iNaturalist. The main Places-LT Ours rows change from 50.5 to 52.4 for CLIP and from 52.4 to 50.8 for DINOv2. RD/SD results are added and Table 6 is revised. These are changed reported results, without an established explanation for the revisions.

T1.justification: The balanced-error definition, BalCE equations, neighbor-silencing formulation, and classifier restriction are mathematically unchanged; neither version supplies theoretical proofs. Table 1 switches from an imbalance ratio to its reciprocal imbalance-factor convention without changing the underlying datasets or theoretical reasoning.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: granularity benefits long-tail learning, neighboring open-set categories support representation learning, and neighbor-silencing enables their effective use. The new title and removal of numerical highlights from the contribution list do not materially change these claims.

C2.justification: v1 Section 4.3 interprets neighboring auxiliary data alone as harming medium and tail classes through overwhelming their representations. v3 instead distinguishes harmful random data from beneficial selected neighbors, with the proposed method providing further gains. This substantially revises the interpretation of what auxiliary-data selection itself contributes.

D1.justification: v3 newly specifies filtering thresholds of 0.7 and 0.98. The supplied main text no longer states v1's four NVIDIA 3090 GPUs or 3.6 million auxiliary images, but redirects detailed implementation settings to an absent appendix. Consequently, removal versus relocation and the overall extent of reproducibility-detail changes cannot be established.

R1.justification: v3 adds Liu et al.'s work on OOD object detectors and foundation models and removes bibliography entries associated with LA, NCL, BALLAD, GML, Decoder, and ALA. The related-work discussion and positioning against rebalancing, augmentation, and external-resource approaches remain substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: The title changes from Granularity Matters in Long-Tail Learning to Learning from Neighbors: Category Extrapolation for Long-Tail Learning. Terminology, prompts, and Section 4.3 receive localized revisions, but the section order and most methodological, related-work, and concluding prose remain intact.

P2.justification: The document is reformatted throughout from one column to two columns. Figure 1 is rearranged into a two-by-two panel layout, Tables 2 and 6 are restructured, and v1 Table 3's paired dataset tables become separate tables. The PCA and sensitivity figures are relocated and exchange numbers rather than constituting new visual analyses.

improvement.justification: The new random-versus-selected data controls better isolate the contribution of category selection, and explicit filtering thresholds improve documentation. However, substantial baseline-result reversals lack an explanation of changed settings or corrections, the referenced appendix is unavailable, and the retained direct-classifier discussion no longer matches Table 6. These evidential gains and unresolved consistency and completeness problems prevent a reliable net-quality judgment.
